problem: Existing EQA methods (Das et al. 2018; Wijmans et al. 2019, MP3D-EQA) are end-to-end RL/IL agents trained in simulation. They transfer poorly to real robots, collide with walls, and their VQA heads handle only a closed vocabulary and a few question types ('what color', 'what room').
motivation: Home robots must answer open-vocabulary, diverse questions (e.g. 'where', 'what is') in unseen real houses. Prior ObjectNav work shows that modular, map-based pipelines transfer to the real world far better than end-to-end policies. Foundation models (LLMs, open-vocabulary detectors, VLMs) now make zero-shot perception and QA possible without EQA-specific training.
key_idea: Decompose EQA into zero-shot modules: GPT-3.5 turns the question into a target object category and a declarative caption. A Detic-based semantic map with frontier exploration and A* finds candidate objects. BLIP2 image-text matching decides when the correct target is found and picks the best stored view. LLaVA/BLIP then answers the question on that image.
insight: Navigating toward candidate objects and answering on the view with the highest image-text-matching score consistently beats answering from the start view: Top-1 at T-10 rises from 0.383 to 0.445 and at random starts from 0.305 to 0.368 (Table I). However, the final distance to target d_T stays far above the 1 m stop radius, and at T-10 it sometimes gets worse (3.62/3.60 vs 3.45). So much of the gain comes from selecting a relevant image rather than precise navigation. The hyperparameter sweep favours a lower detection threshold α plus a higher ITM threshold β, i.e. detect liberally and verify with ITM. ROC analysis (figure only) shows BLIP2-MSCOCO with declarative captions is the best ITM model. In the real world, swapping ITM models had minimal impact; failures split across navigation, ITM false negatives, detection misses, VQA errors and multi-room counting.
method: Language understanding: gpt-35-turbo-0613 (Azure) extracts a target object category from the question and rewrites the question as a declarative sentence for image-text matching.

Scene understanding: Detic open-vocabulary segmentation (detection threshold α) on egocentric RGB for the extracted category, projected with depth into a top-down semantic/occupancy map (SemExp implementation).

Planner: training-free frontier-based exploration picks the closest frontier as long-term goal, updated every 25 steps in sim (dynamic in real). Once the category is detected, the object's position becomes the goal. A deterministic A* local policy outputs FORWARD/TURN/STOP; the episode budget is 100 steps.

Image memory + ITM stopping: images are stored when the agent is within 1 m of and facing a detected candidate. BLIP2 (MSCOCO-finetuned) or CLIP scores each image against the declarative sentence, and the agent stops when the score exceeds β.
VQA: the stored image with the highest ITM score is passed with the question to a pretrained VLM (BLIP, BLIP2, or LLaVA-v1.5-7b/13b) for an open-vocabulary answer.

setting.backbone: Modular frozen foundation models: gpt-35-turbo-0613 (question parsing) + Detic (open-vocab segmentation) + BLIP2-MSCOCO/BLIP2-pretrain (ITM) + LLaVA-v1.5-7b or BLIP-pretrain (VQA); frontier exploration + A* (no learned policy)
setting.model_size: LLaVA-v1.5-7B for VQA (13B also tested in VQA-only study); GPT-3.5-turbo size undisclosed
setting.training_data: none (training-free); all components pretrained off-the-shelf. MP3D-EQA train split re-split into train'/val' and used only for model selection and threshold tuning.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (480x640) + pose sensor in sim; stereo camera + 2D LiDAR SLAM on the real robot
setting.action_space: low-level discrete MOVE_FORWARD / TURN_LEFT / TURN_RIGHT / STOP (SemExp/Habitat defaults)
setting.privileged: GT pose sensor in simulation; start positions placed N actions back along the GT shortest path (standard EQA protocol); no GT map or semantics

numbers_note: ITM model comparison (ROC curves) and the VQA-model comparison (BLIP/BLIP2/LLaVA-7b/13b VQA-only Top-1 on MP3D-EQA train') are given only in figures, without numbers. No table compares against prior MP3D-EQA methods (Wijmans et al.). The intro only claims Top-1 'around 0.43, which is higher than the scores stated on existing methods'. The evaluation protocol differs from the original MP3D-EQA: re-split train, original val used as test, and d_T measured at the ITM-selected position. The text reports real-world success as 'around 32' across 19 episodes. The VQA-only baseline's d_T equals the start distance (3.45/4.53/5.71/8.21 m).
results: On MP3D-EQA (original val used as test), the best zero-shot setting (α=0.1, β=0.2, BLIP2-MSCOCO ITM + LLaVA-v1.5-7b) reaches Top-1 0.445/0.434/0.409/0.368 at T-10/T-30/T-50/random starts. The VQA-only-at-start baseline gets 0.383/0.389/0.327/0.305, and d_T improves from 8.21 to 7.73 m at random starts, though still far from the 1 m stop radius. On a real i-CART mini robot in two houses, the method succeeds (correct answer, no collision) in 6–7 of 19 episodes, with 3–4 collisions. Changing the ITM model has little effect there.
limitations: Navigation is weak: d_T remains several meters, far above the 1 m stop distance. Frontier exploration ignores target attributes (colour, location), and detections of foreground object parts cause premature stops.

Real-world success is only about 6–7 of 19 episodes, with 3–4 collisions. Causes are random moves when A* fails and 2D LiDAR SLAM missing obstacles. Counting objects spread across rooms fails for lack of a richer memory.

Evaluation is hard to compare with prior EQA work: custom re-split, d_T measured at the ITM-selected position, only a VQA-only baseline in tables, and unclear matching of free-form answers to GT. The pipeline also relies on a closed GPT-3.5 API.
compares_to: MP3D-EQA end-to-end methods (Wijmans et al. 2019; mentioned in text only)
